procedural_history.impugned_order: Death sentence awarded by the trial court and affirmed by the High Court
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: High Court affirmed the death sentence awarded by the trial court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The applicants filed Criminal Appeals Nos.1396-1397 of 2008, which were dismissed by the Supreme Court on 25.01.2010, maintaining the death sentence. Subsequently, the applicants filed Review Petition (Crl.) Nos.192-193 of 2011, seeking a review of the Supreme Court's judgment. Criminal M.P.Nos.16673-16674 of 2016 and Criminal M.P. Nos.16675-16676 of 2016 were filed in the review petition. The review petitions were ultimately rejected.

issue.issue_text: Whether the power of review can be exercised as an appeal in disguise to rehear and correct an erroneous decision.

law.fact_text: The power of review is not an inherent power of the court; it must be conferred by law, such as under Order 47 Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
relevant_text: It cannot be denied that the review is the creation of a statute. This Court in Patel Narshi Thakershi v. law.fact_text: There is a clear distinction between the power of review and appellate power. Appellate power allows a superior court to correct all errors, whereas review power is much more limited.

application.fact_text: The Court clarified that a review is for correcting a mistake, not for substituting one judicial view for another. The mere possibility that a different conclusion could have been reached on the same facts or law is not a ground for review.
relevant_text: The power of review can be exercised for correction of a mistake but not to substitute a view. reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the proposition, holding that the power of review cannot be exercised as an appeal in disguise. The Court reasoned that a review has a limited and specific purpose: to correct a patent mistake or an error apparent on the face of the record. It is fundamentally different from an appeal and cannot be used to rehear a case, re-appreciate evidence, or substitute a different judicial view simply because the original decision is alleged to be erroneous.

issue.issue_text: Whether a review is maintainable only for a patent error or a material error apparent on the face of the record that results in a miscarriage of justice.

law.law_text: A review is fundamentally different from an appeal. It is not an 'appeal in disguise' where an erroneous decision can be reheard and corrected.
The power of review can only be exercised for a 'patent error' or a 'material error, manifest on the face of the order'.
An 'error apparent on the face of the record' must be self-evident and not one that has to be detected by a process of reasoning or 'fished out and searched'.
The mere possibility of two views on a subject is not a sufficient ground for review; the court cannot substitute one view for another.
To justify a review, the error must be a 'glaring omission or patent mistake' that undermines the soundness of the judgment or results in a 'miscarriage of justice'.

application.application_text: The Supreme Court established a two-part test for a review to be maintainable. First, there must be a specific type of error.

The Court defined this error as being 'patent,' 'material,' and 'apparent on the face of the record.' It clarified that this is a high standard, referring to errors that are self-evident, such as a 'glaring omission or patent mistake,' and not simply an incorrect decision that could be argued differently.

Second, the Court determined that the existence of such an error is not enough on its own. This error must have a significant negative consequence, specifically that it 'results in miscarriage of justice' or 'undermines its soundness'.

By repeatedly stating that a review is not an appeal and is reserved for 'judicial fallibility,' the Court emphasized the limited and exceptional nature of this remedy, thereby accepting that it is only maintainable for a patent or material error apparent on the record that leads to a miscarriage of justice.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that a review is maintainable only when a petitioner can demonstrate the existence of a patent or material error that is apparent on the face of the record. This error must be a grave and obvious mistake, not merely a point that could be argued differently. Crucially, this error must also be so significant that it has resulted in a miscarriage of justice.

issue.issue_text: Whether a review is maintainable when it seeks the same relief that was negatived during the hearing of the main matter.

facts: The applicant in the review petition was seeking the exact same relief that they had previously requested during the hearing of the main matter.
This initial request for relief had been considered and denied (negatived) by the court in its original judgment.
law: A review proceeding is not a rehearing of the original case and cannot be equated with an appeal.

The power of review is not for correcting all errors like an appellate court, but is to be used with extreme caution only in exceptional cases, such as a 'glaring omission or patent mistake' or a 'material error, manifest on the face of the order' that causes a miscarriage of justice.
A review is not maintainable if it is merely a repetition of old and overruled arguments.
A review cannot be used to re-appreciate evidence to reach a different conclusion, nor is the mere possibility of two views on a subject a ground for review.
application: The court applied the principle that a review is not a rehearing of the original case.
It found that the applicant was attempting to re-argue the main matter to obtain a relief that had already been explicitly refused.
The court reasoned that allowing such a review would improperly convert the review process into an appeal or a rehearing of the original case, which is against settled law.
Since the applicant was simply repeating an old argument that had already been considered and rejected, there were no grounds for a review.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that a review petition is not maintainable when it seeks the same relief that was already negatived during the hearing of the main matter. To allow such a review would be to improperly rehear the original case, which is beyond the limited scope of the court's review power.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the power of review can be exercised as an appeal in disguise to rehear and correct an erroneous decision.
appellant_arguments: The applicants (review petitioners) argued for a re-appreciation of the evidence on record to reach a different conclusion than the one in the original judgment.
The applicants sought to argue that the evidence did not support the conclusion reached by the court, which amounts to requesting a rehearing of the appeal.
respondent_arguments: A review petition cannot be converted into an appeal in disguise.
Permitting arguments on the appreciation of evidence during a review is not permissible.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a review is maintainable only for a patent error or a material error apparent on the face of the record that results in a miscarriage of justice.
appellant_arguments: The applicants' submissions did not point out any error apparent on the face of the record, but rather challenged the court's finding of fact based on its appreciation of evidence.
respondent_arguments: A conclusion on facts reached by an appellate court cannot be assailed in a review petition unless there is an error apparent on the face of the record.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the mere possibility of two views on the same subject constitutes a sufficient ground for review.
appellant_arguments: The applicants argued that the court should re-appreciate the evidence and reach a different conclusion, implying that an alternative view was possible and should be adopted.
respondent_arguments: It is not open to the court in a review petition to reappreciate evidence and reach a different conclusion, even if another conclusion is possible.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a review petition can be maintained by repeating old and overruled arguments.
appellant_arguments: The applicants raised submissions which the court found did not constitute valid grounds for a review, suggesting a repetition of arguments from the original appeal.
respondent_arguments: A review petition is not maintainable if it does not raise any new grounds for review and merely repeats arguments already considered and rejected.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a review is maintainable when it seeks the same relief that was negatived during the hearing of the main matter.
appellant_arguments: The applicants, by seeking a review of the final judgment dated 25.01.2010, were attempting to have the original judgment and sentence overturned, which was the same relief denied in the criminal appeal.
respondent_arguments: A review cannot be used to re-litigate the case and seek the same relief that was already denied after a full hearing of the appeal.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The power of review can be exercised for the correction of a mistake, but not to substitute a view, and it cannot be treated as an appeal in disguise; the mere possibility of two views on the same subject is not a ground for review.
obiter: The power of review is not an inherent power; it must be conferred by law either specifically or by necessary implication.
Justice is a virtue which transcends all barriers and the rules or procedures or technicalities of law cannot stand in the way of administration of justice.
Law has to bend before justice.
Rectification of an order thus stems from the fundamental principle that justice is above all.
The appreciation of evidence on record is fully within the domain of the appellate court.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court concluded that its review jurisdiction is not an open invitation to re-argue an appeal. The power to review is to be exercised reluctantly and only in specific circumstances, such as when a glaring omission or a patent, material error apparent on the face of the record has resulted in a miscarriage of justice. A review cannot be used as an appeal in disguise to re-appreciate evidence or to advance a different but possible view on the subject, as the applicants attempted to do. Since the submissions raised in the review petitions did not meet this high threshold and merely sought to re-litigate grounds already considered, they did not constitute a valid basis for review.
legal_tests_applied: The power of review is not an inherent power; it must be conferred by law either specifically or by necessary implication.
A review is not an appeal in disguise.
A review is maintainable only when a glaring omission or patent mistake has crept into the earlier decision due to judicial fallibility.
There has to be a material error manifest on the face of the record that results in a miscarriage of justice to exercise the review jurisdiction.
The mere possibility of two views on the same subject is not a ground for review.
why_appellant_lost: By review application an applicant cannot be allowed to re-argue the appeal on the grounds which were urged at the time of the hearing of the criminal appeal.
The submissions raised in the review petitions do not raise any ground for review of the judgment.
Even if the applicant succeeds in establishing that there may be another view possible on the conviction or sentence of the accused that is not a sufficient ground for review.
The appreciation of evidence on record is fully within the domain of the appellate court, it cannot be permitted to be re-examined in a review petition.
why_respondent_won: A review of judgment in a case is a serious step and reluctant resort to it is proper only where a glaring omission or patent mistake or like grave error has crept in earlier by judicial fallibility.
The mere fact that two views on the same subject are possible is no ground to review the earlier judgment passed by a Bench of the same strength.
A review is permissible only when the Court is satisfied that a material error, manifest on the face of the order undermines its soundness or results in miscarriage of justice.
policy_considerations: Rectification of an order thus stems from the fundamental principle that justice is above all. It is exercised to remove the error and not for disturbing finality.

Law has to bend before justice. If the Court finds that the error pointed out in the review petition was under a mistake and the earlier judgment would not have been passed but for erroneous assumption which in fact did not exist and its perpetration shall result in a miscarriage of justice nothing would preclude the Court from rectifying the error.
The indulgence extended in such cases is mainly owing to the natural desire prevailing to prevent irremediable injustice being done by a court of last resort.
The Court is not precluded from recalling or reviewing its own order if it is satisfied that it is necessary to do so for sake of justice or to prevent the abuse of process of court.
